1184.title: Entrusted (Kern ch. 27)
1184.hook: the Buddha entrusts the teaching to the bodhisattvas; the Lotus closed
1184.howItsDone: Communities that keep the Lotus Sutra read its entrustment as the Buddha handing the teaching to the bodhisattvas, and some readers treat reciting, copying or teaching the sutra as a way of taking up that charge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samantabhadra promised to come on a white elephant to anyone who keeps the sutra. Your line: kept and protected.

A set of keys passes from one hand to another. A night nurse walks the morning shift through each patient's chart. A shop changes hands, and the old owner stands in the doorway one last time. Handing something over is its own small ceremony, and the Lotus Sutra ends with one. In the last chapter of Kern's ordering, the Buddha rises from his seat, turns to the great crowd of bodhisattvas, and gives them the teaching to carry.
screen: `KEYS, A CHART, A SHOP.` → `HANDING OVER IS A CEREMONY.` → `THE LOTUS ENDS WITH ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, paraphrased. The Buddha stands, and by his power he reaches out his right hand to the bodhisattvas. Over ages beyond counting, he says, I worked to reach this supreme awakening. Now I hand it to you. Take it, keep it, and make it known widely, so that all beings may hear it. The bodhisattvas bow, filled with joy, and answer together: we will do as the Lord commands. Do not be concerned. And they say it again. Then the Buddha sends home the Buddhas who had gathered from other worlds to hear him, and the assembly rejoices. That's how the Lotus closes, in Kern's order: not with a final parable, but with a handoff. The teaching doesn't stay with the teacher. Look back at the whole Lotus now. A ray of light from the Buddha's brow. Skillful means and one vehicle. A burning house, a lost son, rain falling on every plant. A phantom city to rest in, and a jewel sewn in a coat. A stupa in the sky, and the dragon king's daughter. Bodhisattvas rising from the cracks of the earth, and a Buddha whose life is long beyond counting. Never Disparaging, bowing to everyone. Guanyin hearing cries. Two sons leading a king, and Samantabhadra's promise. And at the end, a hand held out to the listeners: this is yours now.

1185.title: A library of sutras
1185.hook: the Mahayana sutras are many; we read a handful, paraphrased
1185.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia, Tibet and Vietnam chant, study and copy sutras such as the Lotus, the Heart Sutra and the Vimalakirti, and each school tends to center a few of them; the Theravada tradition keeps the Pali canon instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha reached out his hand and handed the Lotus over. Your line: entrusted.

"Thus have I heard." That's how the discourses open in the old English of Rhys Davids, before anyone is named, before a place or a crowd. For weeks this path has stayed inside one book, the Lotus. Today i'm stepping out of it with you to look at the shelf it sits on. It's a long shelf. The Mahayana sutras are many, kept in Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan, and loved in different places for different reasons. Over the coming weeks i'll open a handful.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `ONE BOOK ON A LONG SHELF.` → `A HANDFUL, OPENED.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. A sutra is a discourse: a teaching set in a scene, with a place, a crowd, and someone asking a question. Tradition says that after the Buddha died, his attendant Ananda recited what he had heard, which is why the discourses open with those words. The Mahayana sutras open the same way, and then the scenes grow huge: assemblies of bodhisattvas, light pouring from the Buddha's brow, worlds beyond counting. Different Buddhists hold these books differently, so here, plainly, is who holds what. Mahayana traditions in China, Tibet, Korea, Japan and Vietnam receive these sutras as the Buddha's word. The Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia keeps its own canon in Pali, and these Mahayana sutras aren't part of it. Historians tell their own story about when and where the texts were written. This path tells each text as it tells itself, and names the differences without ranking anyone. Now the shelf ahead. A sick layman in the city of Vaishali who out-talks the Buddha's great disciples, and a goddess who scatters flowers in his room. A sutra that pictures the universe as a net of jewels, and a young pilgrim who visits teacher after teacher. A finger pointing at the moon. A Buddha of medicine, a bodhisattva who vows to empty the hells, and a queen named Srimala who teaches. One honest note: i'll mostly retell these in my own words, because the English translations i'd want to quote aren't ones i can share freely. When i paraphrase, i'll say so.

1186.title: Vimalakirti is ill
1186.hook: a wealthy layman of Vaishali lies sick, and the Buddha wants someone to visit him
1186.howItsDone: The Vimalakirti Sutra is read across Mahayana traditions, and in East Asia Vimalakirti became a model of the lay practitioner: someone with a household and a job whose practice is carried out in ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long shelf of sutras, each opening with thus have I heard. Your line: a library. Now the first book comes down.

In the city of Vaishali, a rich man is in bed, sick. Word gets around, and the visitors start coming: princes and ministers, merchants, townspeople, priests and householders. He's glad to see every one of them, and from his sickbed, propped on the pillows, he teaches them. His name is Vimalakirti. The sutra named for him, one of the books Kumarajiva put into Chinese, says something odd right away. His illness is a skillful means. He is sick on purpose, for the sake of the people who come to see him.
screen: `A RICH MAN SICK IN VAISHALI.` → `THE VISITORS KEEP COMING.` → `SICK FOR THEIR SAKE.`

segments.voice: First, who he is. Vimalakirti isn't a monk. He's a householder, with a wife and children, servants, money, and a place in the life of his city. The sutra shows him moving through all of it: the markets, the law courts, the schools, even the gambling halls and the drinking houses. He keeps a householder's clothes and a householder's life, and everywhere he goes, the sutra says, he's there to bring people toward the teaching: a layman whose wisdom matches the great bodhisattvas. That's this book's first surprise. Now the sickbed. When the visitors come, he doesn't talk about his fever. He talks about the body. It's like a ball of foam that can't be squeezed, he tells them. Like a bubble that doesn't last. Like a mirage, a dream, a reflection, like the trunk of a plantain tree, with no hard core inside. A list meant to unsettle. But listen to where he takes it. He doesn't tell them to despise the body. He tells them to turn toward a different kind of body, the body of a Buddha, made of generosity, patience, wisdom and kindness. The sick body becomes a door. Then the scene turns. Lying there, Vimalakirti thinks: I'm sick. Won't the Buddha send someone to ask after me? And the Buddha, knowing his thought, turns to his disciples and asks who will go. That's tomorrow's story.

1187.title: No one wants to go
1187.hook: one by one the great disciples decline, each remembering being out-argued by him
1187.howItsDone: Some teachers in Mahayana traditions use these refusal stories to teach that practice is not limited to the forest or the meditation hall, and that a layperson's insight can match a monk's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vimalakirti lay sick in Vaishali, teaching his visitors that the body is like foam. Your line: the sick layman.

The Buddha asks a simple favor: go and ask after Vimalakirti; he's ill. He turns first to Shariputra, the disciple known for wisdom. And Shariputra says, as the sutra tells it: I'm not fit to go. Then he explains why, with a story about himself coming off badly. The Buddha turns to the next disciple, and the next. Each one says no. Each one has a story, and every story is told by the one who lost the argument.
screen: `A SIMPLE FAVOR.` → `I'M NOT FIT TO GO.` → `EACH ONE HAS A STORY.`

segments.voice: Here are a few of the stories, paraphrased. Shariputra remembers sitting quietly under a tree in the forest, deep in meditation. Vimalakirti came by and told him: that isn't the way to sit. Sit without withdrawing from the world. Sit while doing the ordinary things of life, without leaving behind the people around you. Shariputra had no answer, so he stayed silent. Maudgalyayana remembers teaching a crowd of householders in the street; Vimalakirti stopped him and said the teaching can't be handed out the way he was handing it out. Mahakashyapa remembers going only to poor houses for alms, to give the poor a chance to earn merit. Vimalakirti told him to beg from everyone alike, rich and poor. And then Ananda. The Buddha had been unwell, and Ananda went to a house to fetch some milk. Vimalakirti met him at the door: hush, the Buddha's body is the body of the teaching; don't let anyone hear you say he's sick. Ananda was mortified. Then a voice from the sky said: Ananda, the layman is right. But go and take the milk, and don't be ashamed. Look at what the sutra is doing. These are the great disciples, the names at the center of the older discourses, and each one remembers being out-argued by a householder, and says so in front of everyone. Then even the bodhisattvas decline, Maitreya among them. Each refusal makes the visit sound harder. The sutra is clearing the room for someone.

1188.title: Manjushri visits
1188.hook: the bodhisattva of wisdom goes; the room holds countless seats
1188.tomorrow: I'm sick because the world is sick
1188.howItsDone: Across Mahayana traditions Manjushri is honored as the bodhisattva of wisdom, shown in images with a sword and a book, and the meeting of Manjushri and Vimalakirti appears in East Asian painting and teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great disciples refused to visit the sick layman, each one remembering being out-argued. Your line: they all declined.

Finally the Buddha turns to Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. Manjushri doesn't pretend it will be easy. Vimalakirti is hard to answer, he says; he sees deep into the teaching, and his speech is quick. But I'll go. The moment he agrees, the whole assembly wants to come along: bodhisattvas, disciples, gods. Two great minds in one sickroom; nobody wants to miss that. So a vast crowd follows Manjushri into the city, toward one small house.
screen: `HE IS HARD TO ANSWER.` → `BUT I'LL GO.` → `A VAST CROWD FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: Vimalakirti sees them coming and does something strange. By his power he empties his house. The attendants go, the furniture goes, and nothing is left but the one bed he lies on. Manjushri walks in, and Vimalakirti greets him with a riddle. Welcome, Manjushri. You've come without coming, and you appear without being seen. Manjushri answers in kind: so it is. What has already come doesn't come again, and what has gone doesn't go again. They're talking about emptiness before anyone has sat down. And nobody can sit down. A little later in the visit, Shariputra looks around the bare room and wonders where all these people are supposed to sit. Vimalakirti reads his thought and teases him. Did you come here for the teaching, or for a chair? Then he solves it anyway. He asks Manjushri where the finest lion thrones in all the worlds are found, and Manjushri names a Buddha in a far-off world. Vimalakirti calls for those thrones, and they arrive, enormous, towering, and fit into his small room without crowding it. The city outside isn't crowded either. The bodhisattvas grow tall enough to take their seats; the disciples can't climb up until they bow to the Buddha the thrones came from. The sutra calls this kind of thing an inconceivable liberation. The house didn't get bigger on the outside. It just made room.

1189.title: I'm sick because the world is sick
1189.word: I'm sick because the world is sick
1189.hook: Vimalakirti says his illness comes from compassion for sick beings
1189.howItsDone: In Mahayana traditions this passage is read as a picture of the bodhisattva's compassion, and caring for the sick is taught as part of the bodhisattva path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Manjushri walked into an emptied sickroom, and lion thrones fit inside without crowding it. Your line: the room grows.

Is it bearable? Is it getting better, or worse? Those are the questions anyone asks at a bedside, and they're the ones Manjushri asks first. He passes on a message, too: the Buddha asks after you. Then the deeper questions. Where does this sickness come from? How long will it last? How will it end? Vimalakirti's answer doesn't sound like a medical report at all. It sounds like a confession of love.
screen: `IS IT BEARABLE?` → `THE BUDDHA ASKS AFTER YOU.` → `WHERE DOES THIS SICKNESS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Here's his answer, paraphrased. From ignorance comes craving, and from that comes my sickness. Because all beings are sick, I am sick. When beings are no longer sick, my sickness will end. A bodhisattva enters the round of birth and death for the sake of beings, he explains, and wherever there's birth and death, there's sickness. Then a picture from family life. A householder has an only child. When the child falls ill, the parents fall ill with worry; when the child gets well, so do they. A bodhisattva loves beings like that, as if each were an only child. Then what is the cause of your sickness, Manjushri asks. And Vimalakirti says: it comes from great compassion. He isn't claiming to have caught everyone's flu. A heart open to the world can't stay untouched by the world's pain; the sickness is the cost of staying close. Then a practical question: how should one bodhisattva comfort another who is sick? The answer is gentle. Speak of the body's impermanence, but not of disgust for the body. Speak of suffering, but don't urge an escape into a private peace. Remember your own past pains, and think of the pains of others. And be a physician: heal others' sickness, and your own along with it. In this sutra, the sickroom isn't a detour from the path. It's where the teaching happens.

1190.title: The goddess and the flowers
1190.hook: flowers fall on everyone; they slide off the bodhisattvas but stick to the disciples who think flowers improper
1190.howItsDone: Teachers in Mahayana traditions use the goddess and the flowers to talk about attachment to distinctions, while monastic communities in these traditions continue to keep their precepts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vimalakirti said his illness comes from great compassion, like a parent sick beside a sick child. Your line: because the world is sick.

Petals begin to drift down from nowhere, over the whole crowded room. Someone in Vimalakirti's house has been listening all along: a goddess who lives there. She's so delighted by what she's heard that she shows herself and scatters heavenly flowers over everyone, bodhisattvas and disciples alike. It should be a lovely moment. For some of the guests, it is. For others, it turns into a small, very public struggle with a flower.
screen: `PETALS FROM NOWHERE.` → `A GODDESS WHO LIVES IN THE HOUSE.` → `A STRUGGLE WITH A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's what happens, paraphrased. The flowers touch the bodhisattvas and fall away. On the great disciples, they stick. Shariputra tries to brush them off his robe. They stay. The others try, even using their powers. They stay. So the goddess asks him, mildly: why are you trying to get rid of them? Flowers aren't proper for a monk, Shariputra says. He means the monastic rule against adornment; a monk doesn't wear garlands. The goddess answers: don't call the flowers improper. The flowers don't think about proper and improper. You're the one making that distinction, and for someone who has left home for the teaching, clinging to distinctions like that is what's out of place. The flowers don't stick to the bodhisattvas, because they've let go of those distinctions. Then a picture. When someone is afraid, harmful spirits find an opening; when fear is gone, nothing can get a grip. In the same way, the things of the senses cling to those who are afraid of them, and slide off those who aren't. Some readers hear a hard question about rules here. The goddess isn't telling monks to throw out their precepts. Her target is the gripping: holding a rule so tightly that a gift from the sky becomes a stain. It's the week's last day, so look back. The Lotus entrusted. A library of sutras opened. A sick layman, disciples who all declined, a room that grew, a sickness born of compassion, and now flowers that stick only where someone is pushing them away.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one of your own small rules, not a deep moral line: how the dishwasher gets loaded, where the shoes go. Notice how tightly you hold it, and the little flare when someone breaks it. On an out-breath, loosen the grip slightly, like opening a fist; the rule can stay, only the grip changes.
